doc.title: Greg Caputo interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 14, 1998

chapter: Playing styles, cruises and tribute bands
title: Responsibility in the Artie Shaw and Benny Goodman bands
summary: He feels the weight of Buddy Rich's and Gene Krupa's chairs, and a fan mistakes him for Gene Krupa.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: They make you help with shuffleboard now, huh? Well can you tell me about, you said the Benny Goodman Big Band is coming up and I know you’ve done some of that in the past.

Yeah I was quite flattered. I can remember sitting in the Artie Shaw Band for the first time and opening the book and see that signature of Buddy Rich in there, and it hit me in a big way, that I had forgotten that he had sat in that chair. And the responsibility was, when Dick Johnson would announce that Buddy Rich was with the band and he used to solo, he used to change the tunes, “Lady Be Good,” there was a responsibility there I felt, to Buddy, to do the best I can. And I always like got plenty of rest, ate well and practiced © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

myself to death because I had a responsibility there. And with the Benny Goodman Band of course one of my favorite drummers, Gene Krupa was with that band, and I also feel a responsibility to that. I can remember playing, we did a sextet job, a small band with vibes and someone came up to me and they said, “Gene, you look great.” Because my initials are GC and they just assumed it was Gene Krupa. And, “You’re playing better than ever.” Well I didn’t think and I responded, “Well thank you very much but Gene has passed on.” And the person was devastated. They were devastated over this. And the leader of the band pulled me over and he said, “Never, ever — you’re whoever they want you to be. They come and they’re living a dream, and don’t ever say anybody passed on.” So there’s a responsibility there.
Yeah. That’s significant, that they’re living a dream that this music made such an impression on them in their younger years. It’s important that they hear it like they remember it I guess.

Yes. I say to some of the musicians that take these jobs, don’t do that. If you’re playing swing music, you’re not playing bebop. I mean there’s a difference there and you have a responsibility. And as a result they go through a lot of musicians in these bands. You have to know the style. So if you get a call, do your homework.
